pairs.why: In A the tabletop, board grid, pedestal and stool tops all read from the same raised camera, while B's tabletop and board tilt toward the viewer more steeply than its level-looking stools and pedestal base.

B's crossed legs meet at a central hinge, and its arms and back fabric attach to the frame poles, while in A the back uprights and the front X-legs never join cleanly to the seat rails and bottom runner.

B's tabletop, pedestal base and stool tops share one viewing angle and sensible sizes, while A's tiny table sits almost level with its stools and its top looks tipped up more steeply than the pedestal.
The two lassos are nearly identical, and in both the big loop's path into the coil at the ferrule is equally ambiguous.
Both chess tables use almost the same camera and construction, with the pedestal on its base, stools on the grass and the board grid following the tabletop, so neither is clearly more correct.

A's yoke hangs from one clamp-and-stem on the truss and pivots on both sides of the lamp, a believable mount, while B's yoke clamps to the lower truss chord with its left pivot hidden and only loosely attached.
In B the truss clamp, yoke pivot and lamp face ellipse all match one camera, while A's flat, front-on truss doesn't match its lamp seen from below, and A's yoke joins the lamp on only one side.

A's yoke grips the lamp at pivots on both sides and its front lens ellipse matches the body, while B's left yoke arm ends at the lamp with no pivot and its stretched body doesn't line up with its face.
